# Welcome {.unnumbered}

Modal is a MIDI sequencer for Linux and Windows, designed to let you write,
arrange and shape music from the keyboard. Its window uses a fixed character
grid, but it is a graphical application: the piano roll, arrangement and event
list are different views of the same song.

This book assumes you know what MIDI tracks, notes, channels and controllers
are. It assumes **no knowledge of Vim**, the keyboard-driven text editor
whose command language inspired Modal's editing model. Vim combines actions
with descriptions of text; Modal applies that idea to musical things such
as notes, bars and sections. This book explains the model in musical terms.

## About this edition {.unnumbered}

This is the initial draft of Modal's user manual. It documents the implemented behaviour of Modal
0.1.0, based on application revision `99d70a7`
(16 November 2026). This draft was accepted on 16 November 2026;
the manual is maintained alongside application development on `main`.

The chapters progress from orientation and editing grammar to note entry,
arrangement, recording, performance shaping, controllers and efficient work.
Configuration and file exchange follow, with compact key tables and generated
transform and settings references at the back. Planned features such as
Insert-mode step entry and loop recording are not presented as available.

## Reading this book {.unnumbered}

Start with @sec-first-session. The chapters build up the ideas behind the
interface and the editing language, with examples whose results are explained
in the text. They can be read away from a computer. Having Modal open is
optional: it lets you explore those ideas as you encounter them.

The emphasis is on what an action means and when it is useful. Key mnemonics
are explained where they help, so the keyboard becomes a language you can
understand and recall.

The examples use the default key bindings. If you already have a customised
`modalrc`, your bindings may differ. The hint menus and the list of keys show
the bindings active in your session.

The illustrations and examples use [First phrase](examples/first-phrase.modal),
an example song you can also download. With the PDF, use
`docs/manual/examples/first-phrase.modal` in the source checkout,
or the `examples` folder beside the generated online manual. The song has
two tracks, Melody and Bass, and two four-bar sections, Phrase and Answer,
in 4/4 at 100 BPM. It contains no device-specific
port names or program changes.

## How keys are written {.unnumbered}

`h` means press the letter h. `G` means a capital G. `gg` means press g twice,
one key after the other. `Ctrl-P` means hold Ctrl while pressing p. `Shift-Tab`
means hold Shift while pressing Tab.

Spaces between key names in an explanation separate steps; do not type spaces
unless the book says **Space**. Thus `,` then `?` opens the list of keys, and
`>` then `i` then `b` is written `>ib` once you know the sequence.

A command written `:grid 1/8` means press `:`, type `grid 1/8`, then press Enter.
You do type the space between the command and its argument. The leading colon
opens Modal's own command line; it is not a command for your operating system's
terminal.

> **Cancellation and undo serve different purposes.** Escape cancels a waiting
> key sequence or leaves a prompt. `u` undoes an accepted musical edit while
> the keys are acting as commands. Cancelling a prompt does not undo an edit
> that has already been accepted.
